etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English or; partially contracted from other, auther, from Old English āþor, āwþer, āhwæþer ("some, any, either"; > either); and partially from Middle English oththe, from Old English oþþe, from Proto-Germanic *efþau (“or”).

definitions.definition: Connects at least two alternative words, phrases, clauses, sentences, etc., each of which could make a passage true.
(logic) An operator denoting the disjunction of two propositions or truth values. There are two forms, the inclusive or and the exclusive or.
Counts the elements before and after as two possibilities.
Otherwise (a consequence of the condition that the previous is false).

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter IV, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC, page 46:
quote.text: No matter how early I came down, I would find him on the veranda, smoking cigarettes, or otherwise his man would be there with a message to say that his master would shortly join me if I would kindly wait.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From late Middle English or (“gold”), borrowed from Middle French or (“yellow”), from Old French or, from Latin aurum (“gold”). Doublet of aurum.

definitions.definition: (heraldry) The gold or yellow tincture on a coat of arms.

quote.citation: 1909, Arthur Charles Fox-Davies, A Complete Guide to Heraldry:
quote.text: The metals are gold and silver, these being termed "or" and "argent".

quote.citation: 1889, Charles Norton Elvin, A Dictionary of Heraldry:
quote.text: In engraving, "Or" is expressed by dots.

definitions.definition: (heraldry) Of gold or yellow tincture on a coat of arms.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Late Old English ār, from Old Norse ár. Compare ere.

definitions.definition: (now archaic or dialect) Before; ere. Followed by "ever" or "ere".

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Ecclesiastes 12:6-7:
quote.text: Or euer the siluer corde be loosed, or the golden bowle be broken, or the pitcher be broken at the fountaine, or the wheele broken at the cisterne. Then shall the dust returne to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall returne vnto God who gaue it.

quote.citation: 1834, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, The Rime of the Ancient Mariner:
quote.text: I looked to heaven, and tried to pray;But or ever a prayer had gusht,A wicked whisper came, and madeMy heart as dry as dust.

quote.citation: 1906, Lord Dunsany [i.e., Edward Plunkett, 18th Baron of Dunsany], Time and the Gods‎[2], London: William Heineman, →OCLC, page 3:
quote.text: And Time went forth into the worlds to obey the commands of the gods, yet he cast furtive glances at his masters, and the gods distrusted Time because he had known the worlds or ever the gods became.
